title: Python Next Steps: Data and Files
summary: Go beyond the basics: store data in dictionaries, tidy text, save and load files and CSV, handle errors, and finish with a small grade book project.
audience: Learners aged 14 and up who have finished an introductory Python course (variables, loops, lists and functions)

body.p: In the introduction you stored many values in a list and found them by position: scores[0], scores[1]. Often a label is easier to remember than a number. A dictionary stores pairs, each made of a key and a value, and you look up a value by its key. Think of a price list at a market stall: the key is the item and the value is the price in naira, cedis, shillings or pounds.

body.code:
prices = {"rice": 1200, "beans": 900, "garri": 450}
print(prices["beans"])
prices["yam"] = 1500      # add a new pair
prices["rice"] = 1300     # change an existing value
print(len(prices))
print(prices.get("bread", 0))

body.p: Square brackets with a key read or set a value. Reading a key that does not exist stops the program with a KeyError, so use .get(key, default) when the key might be missing: it returns the default instead. Here bread is not in the dictionary, so .get gave 0.
The .items() method gives you each key and value together, so you can unpack them into two loop variables.

body.code:
rice 1300
beans 900
garri 450
Total: 2650

body.p: To count how often things appear, use the item as the key and the count as the value. The line counts.get(w, 0) + 1 means: take the old count (or 0 if we have not seen this word) and add one.

body.code: {'goal': 3, 'pass': 2, 'shot': 1}

body.p: A tuple is written with round brackets. It works like a list, but once made it cannot be changed. That makes it a good fit for values that belong together, such as a map position or a name with a mark. You can unpack a tuple into separate variables in one line.

body.code:
point = (3, 5)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
print(point[0])

point = (3, 5)
point[0] = 9
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

check.e: get returns the default you give it (0) when the key is missing, instead of crashing like prices["yam"] would.

body.p: A set is written with curly brackets but has no pairs. It keeps each item only once and has no fixed order, so do not rely on position. Sets are excellent for removing duplicates and for asking who is in both groups. Below, two classes sign up for a quiz club. The sorted function puts the answer in a predictable order for display.

body.code:
['Kofi', 'Zainab']
['Ama', 'Kofi', 'Wanjiru', 'Zainab']
['Ama']
3

list: Dictionary { }: pairs, look up by key, changeable.
Set { }: unique items, no order, fast membership checks with the word in.
List [ ]: ordered and changeable, duplicates allowed.

check.e: A set keeps only unique items, so the repeated "a" is stored once: a, b and c.

body.tip: An empty pair of curly brackets {} makes an empty dictionary, not an empty set. To make an empty set write set().

body.p: Text is called a string, and strings come with built-in tools called methods. You call a method with a dot after the value. Real data is messy: names typed with extra spaces, capital letters in odd places. These methods clean it up. Remember that strings cannot be changed, so each method returns a new string and you must print it or store it in a variable.

body.code:
name = "  chidi OKAFOR  "
print(name.strip())
print(name.strip().title())
print(name.upper())
print(name.strip().lower().replace("o", "0"))

chidi OKAFOR
Chidi Okafor
  CHIDI OKAFOR  
chidi 0kaf0r

list: strip() removes spaces and line breaks from both ends.
lower(), upper() and title() change capital letters.
replace(old, new) swaps every occurrence of old for new.
startswith(text) and endswith(text) answer True or False.

body.p: Data often arrives as one line with separators, for example a mark list from a teacher. split(",") breaks the line into a list of strings, and "-".join(list) glues a list back together. Notice that the numbers are still text after splitting. Adding two strings joins them, so convert with int() before doing arithmetic.

body.code:
line = "Ama,72,85,64"
parts = line.split(",")
print(parts)
print("-".join(parts))
print(parts[1] + parts[2])
print(int(parts[1]) + int(parts[2]))

email = "ama@school.edu.gh"
print("@" in email)
print(email.endswith(".gh"))
print(email.find("@"))
print(email[:3])
print(len(email))

True
True
3
ama
17

body.p: The word in checks whether a piece of text appears inside another. find returns the position of the first match, counting from 0, or -1 if there is no match. The slice email[:3] means the first three characters.

check.e: split gives strings, so + joins "72" and "85". Use int() on each part to add them as numbers.

body.p: Put the letter f before the opening quote and write variables inside curly brackets. After a colon you can add a format: .1f means one digit after the decimal point, a comma adds thousands separators, and .0% turns 0.78 into 78%. The symbols < and > left-align or right-align inside a fixed width, which makes neat columns.

body.code:
name = "Wanjiru"
mark = 78.456
fee = 1250000
print(f"{name} scored {mark:.1f}")
print(f"Fee: {fee:,}")
print(f"Pass rate: {0.78456:.0%}")
print(f"|{name:<10}|{mark:>8.2f}|")

Wanjiru scored 78.5
Fee: 1,250,000
Pass rate: 78%
|Wanjiru   |   78.46|

check.e: :.0% multiplies by 100, rounds to 0 decimal places and adds a % sign.

body.tip: When a program prints a number you did not expect, print the value with repr(value) or print(type(value)). It quickly shows whether you have text or a number, and whether hidden spaces are present.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files and CSV

body.p: Variables vanish when a program ends. Files keep data on the phone or computer so the next run can use it. You open a file with open(name, mode). The mode "w" writes (and erases anything already there), "a" appends to the end, and "r" reads (the default). Always use the with statement: it closes the file for you, even if something goes wrong, so data is saved properly.

body.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Maths\n")
    f.write("English\n")

with open("notes.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Biology\n")

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

Maths
English
Biology

body.p: write does not add a line break by itself, so we added \n at the end of each line. When reading line by line, each line still carries its \n, which is why strip() is used. You can also read everything at once with read(). Using repr shows the hidden line-break characters.

body.code:
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()
print(repr(text))
print(len(text.splitlines()))

'Maths
English
Biology
'
3

check.q: You want to add a new line to the end of notes.txt without losing what is already there. Which mode do you open it in?
check.e: "w" empties the file first, and "r" only reads. "a" adds to the end.

body.p: CSV means comma-separated values. It is the simple table format that spreadsheet apps such as Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice can open and save. Each line is a row and commas separate the columns. Python's csv module handles tricky cases for you, such as a comma inside a name. Open CSV files with newline="" as shown.

body.code:
import csv

rows = [["name", "score"], ["Ama", 72], ["Kofi", 85], ["Zainab", 91]]
with open("scores.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerows(rows)

with open("scores.csv") as f:
    print(f.read())

name,score
Ama,72
Kofi,85
Zainab,91

body.p: Reading with csv.DictReader is friendlier because each row becomes a dictionary using the first line as the keys. Everything read from a file is text, so convert the score with int() before adding to it.

body.code:
import csv

with open("scores.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], int(row["score"]) + 5)

Ama 77
Kofi 90
Zainab 96

body.p: To write dictionaries use csv.DictWriter, which needs the column names and writeheader() for the first line.

body.code:
import csv

data = [{"item": "bus fare", "amount": 200}, {"item": "airtime", "amount": 500}]
with open("spend.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["item", "amount"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(data)

with open("spend.csv") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

item,amount
bus fare,200
airtime,500

check.q: csv.DictReader reads a row where the score column holds 72. What is row["score"]?
check.e: CSV files store text, so every value arrives as a string. Convert with int(row["score"]) before doing maths.

body.tip: Mode "w" erases the old file the moment you open it. If you want to keep earlier data, read it first or use "a".

lessons.title: Handling errors with try and except

body.p: Every programmer sees errors. An error that is not handled stops the whole program, which is a poor experience for a user who typed a letter instead of a number. The try and except statement lets you attempt something risky and decide what to do if it fails. The code under try runs normally. If an error of the named kind happens, Python jumps to the except block instead of crashing.

body.code:
text = "abc"
try:
    n = int(text)
    print("Number:", n)
except ValueError:
    print("That is not a whole number")
print("Program continues")

That is not a whole number
Program continues

body.p: Name the error you expect. A bare except that catches everything can hide real bugs. Common ones are ValueError (right type, wrong content, such as int("abc")), ZeroDivisionError, KeyError (missing dictionary key), IndexError (list position too big) and FileNotFoundError (file does not exist).
You can add one except block per error type. An optional else block runs only when nothing went wrong, which keeps the success path separate.

body.code:
Ama scored 72
Wanjiru is not in the register

body.h: Asking until the answer is valid

body.p: A very useful pattern is a loop that keeps asking until the input is acceptable. In this run the user types abc, then -5, then 42. We feed those three answers in automatically so you can see the result; on your own device you would type them.

body.code:
Please type digits only
Age cannot be negative
Age saved: 42

check.e: int("12a") raises ValueError, so the except block runs. The else block only runs when no error happened.

body.code: No saved data yet, starting fresh

check.q: Opening a file that does not exist for reading raises which error?
check.e: Catch FileNotFoundError to start fresh when there is no saved data yet.

body.tip: Do not use try and except to hide mistakes in your own logic. Use it for things outside your control: user typing, missing files, bad data.

body.p: A very common job is to build a new list from an old one. With a loop you need three or four lines. A list comprehension does the same in one line, and Python programmers use it all the time. The shape is [what to keep for item in collection]. Read it from left to right as a sentence: give me this, for each item in that.

body.code:
marks = [45, 72, 38, 91, 60]

doubled = []
for m in marks:
    doubled.append(m * 2)
print(doubled)

print([m * 2 for m in marks])

body.p: Both versions produce the same list. The second is shorter once you are used to it. You can add an if at the end to keep only some items, like a filter.

body.code:
marks = [45, 72, 38, 91, 60]
passed = [m for m in marks if m >= 50]
print(passed)
print(len(passed))
print([m + 5 for m in marks if m < 50])

names = ["  ama", "KOFI ", "zainab"]
clean = [n.strip().title() for n in names]
print(clean)
lengths = [len(n) for n in clean]
print(lengths)

['Ama', 'Kofi', 'Zainab']
[3, 4, 6]

body.p: To change each item in one of two ways, put an if and else before the for. Compare this with the filter above: a filter has the if at the end and may make the list shorter, while the choice version has the if first with an else and keeps the same number of items.

body.code:
marks = [45, 72, 38, 91]
print(["pass" if m >= 50 else "fail" for m in marks])
['fail', 'pass', 'fail', 'pass']

check.e: The if at the end keeps only the marks that are 50 or more.
check.code: print([m for m in [45, 72, 38, 91] if m >= 50])

body.p: The same idea works with curly brackets. A dictionary comprehension needs key: value, and a set comprehension removes duplicates automatically.

body.code:
names = ["Ama", "Kofi", "Zainab"]
print({n: len(n) for n in names})
print(sorted({len(n) for n in names}))

check.e: A dictionary comprehension builds key: value pairs, here each name and its length.

body.tip: If a comprehension becomes hard to read, write the ordinary loop instead. Clear code is better than short code.

body.p: Python ships with a large standard library: ready-made tools grouped in modules. You bring a module in with import, then use its tools with a dot. You can also import only what you need with from. None of the modules in this lesson need to be installed. They arrive with Python.

The statistics module calculates summaries of data. Mean is the sum divided by the count, median is the middle value once sorted (the average of the two middle values if there is an even count), and mode is the most common value.

body.code:
import statistics

scores = [60, 70, 70, 80, 95]
print(statistics.mean(scores))
print(statistics.median(scores))
print(statistics.mode(scores))
print(max(scores) - min(scores))
from statistics import median
print(median([7, 1, 9, 3]))

body.p: The random module makes unpredictable choices, useful for quiz games, picking a winner or shuffling questions. Your output will differ each time you run it, so we check results using comparisons that are always true instead of copying a value. random.randint(1, 6) includes both ends, like a dice. random.choice picks one item from a list, and random.shuffle mixes a list in place.

body.code:
import random

roll = random.randint(1, 6)
print(1 <= roll <= 6)

winner = random.choice(["Ama", "Kofi", "Zainab"])
print(winner in ["Ama", "Kofi", "Zainab"])

cards = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
random.shuffle(cards)
print(sorted(cards))

True
True
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

body.p: If you call random.seed(10) before using random, the same numbers come out each time on the same Python version. That is handy for testing a program.

check.e: Sorted, the list is 1, 3, 7, 9. With an even count the median is the mean of the middle two: (3 + 7) / 2 = 5.0.

body.p: Dates are tricky to handle by hand because months have different lengths. The datetime module does the work. A date is made from year, month and day. Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta, and .days gives the number of days. strftime turns a date into text; %A is the weekday name, %d the day, %B the month name and %Y the year.

body.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta

today = date(2026, 10, 7)
exam = date(2026, 12, 18)
print((exam - today).days)
print(today.strftime("%A %d %B %Y"))
print(today + timedelta(days=30))
print(exam > today)

72
Wednesday 07 October 2026
2026-11-06
True

body.p: To get the real current date use date.today(). We used a fixed date above so that your output matches ours.

check.e: Subtracting two dates gives a timedelta; .days is the number of days between them.
check.code:
from datetime import date
print((date(2026, 12, 18) - date(2026, 12, 1)).days)

body.tip: When Python says ModuleNotFoundError, check the spelling first. Names are case sensitive: random, not Random.

body.p: Now we combine everything into a small real program: a grade book that saves marks in a CSV file, loads them next time, handles a missing file, and prints a report. Plan before coding. We need: a dictionary of student to mark; a function to save; a function to load; a function to turn a mark into a grade; and a report that uses f-strings and the statistics module.

steps: Store marks in a dictionary: name as key, mark as value.
Write save_scores to write the dictionary to gradebook.csv.
Write load_scores to read it back, returning an empty dictionary if the file does not exist.
Write grade to convert a mark into a letter using our own bands.
Write report to print a tidy table and summary.

body.p: Here is the whole program. Our grade bands are just an example for this project: 70 and above is A, 55 and above is B, 40 and above is C, otherwise F. Use your own school's rules in your version.

body.code:
Loaded 0 students
Student    Score  Grade
Ama           72  A
Kofi          58  B
Wanjiru       35  F
Zainab        91  A
Average: 64.0
Highest: Zainab (91)

body.p: Run it a second time in the same folder and the first line will say Loaded 4 students, because the file now exists. That is the power of saving data. In the code, sorted(scores.items()) puts students in alphabetical order, and max(scores, key=scores.get) finds the name with the highest mark.

body.code:
with open("gradebook.csv") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())

student,score
Ama,72
Kofi,58
Zainab,91
Wanjiru,35

check.q: Why does the grade book save scores to a CSV file?
o: So the scores are still there the next time the program runs
Because Python cannot keep numbers in a dictionary
To make the program run faster
check.e: Variables vanish when a program ends. A file keeps the data between runs.

list: Add a function that asks for a name and mark with input() and uses try and except for the mark.
Show how many students passed (40 or more) using a list comprehension.
Switch the project to an expense tracker: key is the item, value is the amount spent, and use statistics.mean for the average spend.
Add a date column using datetime.date.today().

check.e: The sum is 248 and there are 3 students. 248 / 3 = 82.67, which rounds to 82.7.

body.tip: Build and test one function at a time. Run the program after each function so a mistake is easy to find.
